title: Coopers Beach: Shinnecock Beach Access
summary: Coopers Beach stands on the Atlantic shore of Shinnecock homeland. Shinnecock citizens have organized for free access after tribal members faced parking fees and tickets at a beach their families have used for generations. Their proposed solution is direct: recognize a Shinnecock tribal ID for free beach access and parking.
address_label: Coopers Beach, 268 Meadow Lane, Southampton, NY 11968
map_geometry_source: Coopers Beach public entrance at 268 Meadow Lane; point verified against Southampton Village facility information and public map coordinates.
why_this_matters: Beach access is about more than parking. It concerns Shinnecock sovereignty, a continuing relationship with the Atlantic shore, and whether municipal rules recognize that Shinnecock people are not visitors to their own homeland. Accepting tribal ID would provide a clear, dignified way to restore access without forcing tribal citizens to buy permission to reach the coast.
introduction_title: Shinnecock access to the Atlantic shore
introduction_content:
Coopers Beach is part of the Atlantic shoreline within Shinnecock homeland. Shinnecock people have lived with and cared for the Southampton coast from time immemorial. Yet tribal citizens have faced parking fees and tickets while trying to reach this beach, only about a mile from Shinnecock territory.

Shinnecock citizens have asked Southampton Village to restore free access. The proposed solution is practical: a Shinnecock tribal ID should be accepted as proof for free beach entry and parking, or the Village should issue free passes to tribal citizens.
history_title: Beach access, organizing, and the tribal ID solution
history_content:
A continuing relationship with the shore

The ocean is central to Shinnecock life, foodways, work, ceremony, and community memory. Current parking rules divide that continuing relationship from the shoreline by treating Shinnecock citizens as nonresidents, even though Coopers Beach lies within Shinnecock ancestral land.

Campaigns for access

After receiving a parking ticket in 2014, Shinnecock citizen Dyani Brown organized a petition signed by more than 150 tribal citizens and local residents. Southampton Village trustees agreed to review the proposal in 2015, but Brown said communication later stopped. In July 2022, Shinnecock leaders and citizens renewed the effort through letters, public education, social media, and a rally at Coopers Beach.

A direct solution

Shinnecock sovereignty attorney Tela Troge proposed free parking passes or recognition of a Shinnecock Nation membership card at village beaches. Later reporting found that the mayor initially agreed to a plan, but Village trustees rejected it. At that point the Village offered half-price seasonal permits and a limited number of daily passes, which organizers said did not meet what the community asked for.

Where the effort stands

The 2026 guidance published by Southampton Village lists a $55 daily parking pass at Coopers Beach and does not list a Shinnecock tribal-ID exemption. The public rules therefore do not show the requested change as completed. Shinnecock presence at the beach continues: on October 8, 2024, Shinnecock citizens accompanied the Trail of Truth riders to Coopers Beach as part of a cross-country movement for tribal sovereignty and recognition.
